This was probably a result of very limited demagnetization procedures used and for this reason the new study described here has been undertaken. The Buntsandstein sediments of the Holy Cross Mountains contain numerous vertebrate tracks (Ptaszyñski, 2000; Ptaszyñski and NiedŸwiedzki, 2002). The Buntsandstein sediments represent both terrestrial and the marginal marine facies. Such facies usu- ally allow fairly precise sequence stratigraphy correlation. Therefore magnetostratigraphic data should be of importance for dating of these sediments. Good quality palaeomagnetic data can also allow determination of the magnitude of any post-Early Triassic horizontal tectonic rotations in this part of the Holy Cross Mountains. Lower and Middle Buntsandstein sediments from the northern part of the Holy Cross Mountains (Central Poland) were studied palaeomagnetically. The obtained palaeomagnetic pole fits well to the Early Triassic segment of the stable European apparent polar wan- der path. This indicates that there were no detectable horizontal tectonic rotations in this part of the Holy Cross Mountains after the Early Triassic. In the lowermost part of the Buntsandstein sequence (the A0 and A1 units) the basal Triassic normal polarity zone was identi - fied, whereas a reversed polarity dominates in the youngest rocks of the studied sections. This predominantly reversed part can be corre- lated with the Pomorze Formation (lower part of the Middle Buntsandstein). The correlation of these magnetic polarity records with magnetostratigraphic data from the other parts of the Central European Basin as well as from the Tethyan sections shows that in the stud- ied area, the Permian–Triassic boundary should be placed near the boundary between the Top Terrigenous Series (uppermost Zechstein) and the A0 unit (lowermost Buntsandstein). section_candidates.excerpt: . The Buntsandstein sediments of the Holy Cross Mountains contain numerous vertebrate tracks (Ptaszyñski, 2000; Ptaszyñski and NiedŸwiedzki, 2002). The Buntsandstein sediments represent both terrestrial and the marginal marine facies. Such facies usu- ally allow fairly precise sequence stratigraphy correlation. Therefore magnetostratigraphic data should be of importance for dating of these sediments. Good quality palaeomagnetic data can also allow determination of the magnitude of any post-Early Triassic horizontal tectonic rotations in this part of the Holy Cross Mountains. SAMPLING LOCALITIES AND PALAEOMAGNETIC PROCEDURE A total of 72 hand samples for palaeomagnetic studies were collected from the Zechstein to Middle Buntsandstein rocks drilled in the Goleniawy IG 1 vertical borehole. These samples were not azimuthally oriented. The Buntsandstein rocks were also sampled in four outcrops located in the northern region of the Holy Cross Mountains (Fig. 1). The sets from the outcrops contained 23 drill samples (Wióry and Sosnowica outcrops) and 14 hand samples which were collected from the lowermost and uppermost parts of the Lower Buntsandstein (Zache³mie and Sosnowica outcrops), and from the lower part of the Mid- dle Buntsandstein (Czerwona Góra and Wióry outcrops). SStorch Institute of Geology, AS CR, Rozvojov aa 135, 165 00 Praha 6, Czech Republic Abstract The Barrandian area (the Tepl aa-Barrandian unit, Bohemian Massif) provided palaeomagnetic results on Early Palaeozoic rocks and chemical data on siliciclastic sediments of both Middle Cambrian and Early Ordovician to Middle Devonian sedimentary sequences; an outcoming interpretation deﬁned source areas of clastic material and palaeotectonic settings of the siliciclastic rock deposition. The siliciclastic rocks of the earliest Palaeozoic sedimentation cycle, deposited in the Cambrian P rr ııbram-Jince Basin of the Barrandian, were derived from an early Cadomian volcanic island arc developed on Neoproterozoic oceanic lithosphere and ac- creted to a Cadomian active margin of northwestern Gondwana. Inversion of relief terminated the Cambrian sedimentation, and a successory Prague Basin subsided nearby since Tremadocian. Source area of the Ordovician and Early Silurian shallow-marine siliciclastic sediments corresponded to progressively dissected crust of continental arc/active continental margin type of Cadomian age. andian Unit, Bohemian Massif): palaeotectonic implications F. Pato ccka *, P. Pruner, P. SStorch Institute of Geology, AS CR, Rozvojov aa 135, 165 00 Praha 6, Czech Republic Abstract The Barrandian area (the Tepl aa-Barrandian unit, Bohemian Massif) provided palaeomagnetic results on Early Palaeozoic rocks and chemical data on siliciclastic sediments of both Middle Cambrian and Early Ordovician to Middle Devonian sedimentary sequences; an outcoming interpretation deﬁned source areas of clastic material and palaeotectonic settings of the siliciclastic rock deposition. The siliciclastic rocks of the earliest Palaeozoic sedimentation cycle, deposited in the Cambrian P rr ııbram-Jince Basin of the Barrandian, were derived from an early Cadomian volcanic island arc developed on Neoproterozoic oceanic lithosphere and ac- creted to a Cadomian active margin of northwestern Gondwana. Inversion of relief terminated the Cambrian sedimentation, and a successory Prague Basin subsided nearby since Tremadocian. Source area of the Ordovician and Early Silurian shallow-marine siliciclastic sediments corresponded to progressively dissected crust of continental arc/active continental margin type of Cadomian age. The hysteresis after subtraction of the paramagnetic susceptibility shows open loops, indicating that the saturation was not reached. The coercive force ( H c) and the remanent coercive force (Hcr) are high, around 0.33 T and 0.5 T, respectively, indi- cating the presence of high coercive mineral(s), like hema- tite or goethite. The loop shows a slight wasp-wasted shape, which suggests a presence of a lower coercive force component. The wasp-wasted shape of the hysteresis loop obtained with brother samples thermally cleaned in air (Fig. 3 (b)) show the presence of two magnetic phases (Roberts et al., 1995 ). The coercive forces are much smaller (H cf = 0.06 T) in this case, indicating that heating resulted in the formation of a lower coercive force component, very likely magnetite. ChRM was thermally isolated in 117 samples from seven sites. This ChRM ( D = 131.8 , I = 15.7 , k = 196, a95 = 3.8 after dip correction; corresponding pole 29.3 S, 56.4 E) is very similar to that obtained in the neighboring Abadla basin from a formation of the same age. Fold tests associated with progressive unfolding applied to the full merged data from the dated formations of these two basins clearly indicate that the magnetization acquisition predates the deformation, which is attributed to the last phase of the late-Hercynian. The magnetization in these basins is therefore primary or acquired just after deposition. Introduction The main uncertainties in the African Apparent Polar Wander Path (APWP) for the Upper Paleozoic, are related to the lack of suitable formations on the cratonic areas for paleomagnetic studies and the insuﬃcient control of the age of magnetization acquisition. In fact, the age of most paleomagnetic results are not constrained by any paleo- magnetic test as they have been acquired for tabular forma

l., 1995 ), Abadla ( Morel et al., 1981; Merabet et al., 1998 ) and Tindouf ( Merabet et al., 1999; Henry et al., 1999 ) basins within the Saharan craton, but until recently, the only argument for their age of magneti- zation acquisition was the fact that their paleomagnetic direction diﬀered according to the age of the formation. Consequently, none of these formations had been aﬀected by the same magnetic overprint event. Positive reversal tests were also been found in the Jurassic formations of the Illizi basin ( Kies et al., 1995 ), but there were no proofs of the magnetization primary character. Henry et al. (2004) also obtained positive reversal tests for remagnetization of Upper Cenozoic age in several formations in the Illizi basin. In Upper Carboniferous formations, Derder et al. (2001c,d) obtained positive fold test in two diﬀerent areas of the Saharan Craton. Two Upper Carboniferous paleo- magnetic poles have now well-established ages and have similar pole location as the other Upper Carboniferous for- mations. The aim of this paper is to constrain, by fold tests, the age of the paleomagnetic data of the African Autunian formations. section_candidates.excerpt: Introduction The Waterberg Group is a thick Proterozoic sedimentary succession deposited on Archean and Paleoproterozoic rocks of the Kaapvaal Craton (Figure 1), including the ~2.06 Ga Bushveld Complex (Walraven and Hattingh, 1993; Walraven, 1997; de Waal and Armstrong, 2000; Buick et al. , 2001; Eglington and Armstrong, 2004). Rb–Sr and U–Pb dates of ~1.4 to ~1.3 Ga for the Pilanesberg Dyke Swarm and syenite of the Leeuwfontein complex that intrude parts of the group have generally been inferred to provide a younger age limit for the group (e.g. Jansen, 1982; Tankard et al., 1982; Walraven et al., 1990; Emerman, 1991). Widespread dolerite sills that intrude the Waterberg Group and predate Jurassic Karoo magmatism have common

matism in southern Africa and place tighter age constraints on the Waterberg Group than previously available. In South Africa, ~1.88 Ga dolerite intrudes upper Waterberg strata, constraining most, if not all, of the succession to have accumulated between ~2.06 Ga (age of the underlying Bushveld Complex) and ~1.88 Ga. This is consistent with derivation of much of the group from uplifted sources in reactivated segments of the Limpopo Belt. The dolerites are typical continental tholeiites, but their trace-element contents discriminate t hem from dolerite sills of the 1.1 Ga Umkondo Igneous Province, which occur in the same region. Paleomagnetic samples from dolerite intrusions in the Waterberg Group in South Africa (including one sill with a U–Pb baddeleyite age of ~1872 Ma), and from dolerite sills and basalt flows in the Soutpansberg Group to the east-northeast, yield antipodal directions with a site mean pole at 15.6°north, 17.1°east, A 95 = 8.9°. These data are interpreted to indicate that the ~1879 to ~1872 Ma dolerites were intruded into the Waterberg Group during voluminous magmatism associated with development of the Soutpansberg rift basin. Older, ~1927 Ma dolerite in Botswana is similar in age and geochemistry to basalts in the craton-margin Olifantshoek Supergroup, suggesting t

This is consistent with derivation of much of the group from uplifted sources in reactivated segments of the Limpopo Belt. The dolerites are typical continental tholeiites, but their trace-element contents discriminate t hem from dolerite sills of the 1.1 Ga Umkondo Igneous Province, which occur in the same region. Paleomagnetic samples from dolerite intrusions in the Waterberg Group in South Africa (including one sill with a U–Pb baddeleyite age of ~1872 Ma), and from dolerite sills and basalt flows in the Soutpansberg Group to the east-northeast, yield antipodal directions with a site mean pole at 15.6°north, 17.1°east, A 95 = 8.9°. These data are interpreted to indicate that the ~1879 to ~1872 Ma dolerites were intruded into the Waterberg Group during voluminous magmatism associated with development of the Soutpansberg rift basin. Paleomagnetic data for the ~1879 to ~1872 Ma intrusions yield a new Paleoproterozoic pole for the Kaapvaal Craton, and comparisons between the ~1927 and ~1879 to ~1872 Ma post- Waterberg dolerites and broadly coeval mafic rocks elsewhere in South Africa and Zimbabwe help to constrain the nature and temporal and spatial distribution of intraplate Paleoproterozoic magmatism in the region. section_candidates.excerpt: Introduction The Waterberg Group is a thick Proterozoic sedimentary succession deposited on Archean and Paleoproterozoic rocks of the Kaapvaal Craton (Figure 1), including the ~2.06 Ga Bushveld Complex (Walraven and Hattingh, 1993; Walraven, 1997; de Waal and Armstrong, 2000; Buick et al. , 2001; Eglington and Armstrong, 2004). Rb–Sr and U–Pb dates of ~1.4 to ~1.3 Ga for the Pilanesberg Dyke Swarm and syenite of the Leeuwfontein complex that intrude parts of the group have generally been inferred to provide a younger age limit for the group (e.g. Jansen, 1982; Tankard et al., 1982; Walraven et al., 1990; Emerman, 1991). Widespread dolerite sills that intrude the Waterberg Group and predate Jurassic Karoo magmatism have common

matism in southern Africa and place tighter age constraints on the Waterberg Group than previously available. In South Africa, ~1.88 Ga dolerite intrudes upper Waterberg strata, constraining most, if not all, of the succession to have accumulated between ~2.06 Ga (age of the underlying Bushveld Complex) and ~1.88 Ga. This is consistent with derivation of much of the group from uplifted sources in reactivated segments of the Limpopo Belt. The dolerites are typical continental tholeiites, but their trace-element contents discriminate t hem from dolerite sills of the 1.1 Ga Umkondo Igneous Province, which occur in the same region. Paleomagnetic samples from dolerite intrusions in the Waterberg Group in South Africa (including one sill with a U–Pb baddeleyite age of ~1872 Ma), and from dolerite sills and basalt flows in the Soutpansberg Group to the east-northeast, yield antipodal directions with a site mean pole at 15.6°north, 17.1°east, A 95 = 8.9°. These data are interpreted to indicate that the ~1879 to ~1872 Ma dolerites were intruded into the Waterberg Group during voluminous magmatism associated with development of the Soutpansberg rift basin. Older, ~1927 Ma dolerite in Botswana is similar in age and geochemistry to basalts in the craton-margin Olifantshoek Supergroup, suggesting t

This is consistent with derivation of much of the group from uplifted sources in reactivated segments of the Limpopo Belt. The dolerites are typical continental tholeiites, but their trace-element contents discriminate t hem from dolerite sills of the 1.1 Ga Umkondo Igneous Province, which occur in the same region. Paleomagnetic samples from dolerite intrusions in the Waterberg Group in South Africa (including one sill with a U–Pb baddeleyite age of ~1872 Ma), and from dolerite sills and basalt flows in the Soutpansberg Group to the east-northeast, yield antipodal directions with a site mean pole at 15.6°north, 17.1°east, A 95 = 8.9°. These data are interpreted to indicate that the ~1879 to ~1872 Ma dolerites were intruded into the Waterberg Group during voluminous magmatism associated with development of the Soutpansberg rift basin. Older, ~1927 Ma dolerite in Botswana is similar in age and geochemistry to basalts in the craton-margin Olifantshoek Supergroup, suggesting that the mafic magmatism in those two regions is genetically related. Paleomagnetic data for the ~1879 to ~1872 Ma intrusions yield a new Paleoproterozoic pole for the Kaapvaal Craton, and comparisons between the ~1927 and ~1879 to ~1872 Ma post- Waterberg dolerites and broadly coeval mafic rocks elsewhere in South Africa and Zimbabwe help to constrain the nature and temporal and spatial distribution of intraplate Paleoproterozoic magmatism in the region. Stratigraphy and depositional setting of the Waterberg Group The Waterberg Group has been the subject of numerous stratigraphic and sedimentological studies in South Africa, and the following information is primarily from Jansen (1982), Callaghan et al. (1991), van der Neut et al. (1991) and Callaghan (1993). Across the Waterberg plateau and adjacent areas (Figures 2 and 3), the group has a composite stratigraphic thickness of as much as 7km. The lower part of the group there (Swaershoek, Alma and Sterkrivier Formations), and the entire succession exposed in the Middleburg area, consist dominantly of sandstones and rudites (conglomerates and sedimentary breccias) deposited in alluvial fan and fan-delta environments. etic data Paleomagnetic samples were collected at or near the same localities as the geochronological and geochemical samples. Previous experience with similar dolerites in southern Africa indicates that many of these rocks are very strongly magnetized, probably as a result of lightening strikes, and the paleomagnetic samples were therefore oriented with a sun compass and distributed over a large outcrop area. A minimum of nine samples were taken at each site using a gasoline-powered rock drill. Paleomagnetic analyses were carried out at the University of Texas, Austin. IRM (isothermal remanent magnetization) acquisition experiments identify magnetite as the dominant or sole magnetic mineral in all samples (Figure 6a). This is confirmed by thermal demagnetization (Figure 6b), which indicates a broad range of unblocking temperatures below the magnetite Curie point of 580°C. In view of the directional data discussed below, it may be significant that data for sample JP11.12 suggest a second Curie temperature near 450°C, and data for sample WD28.9 suggest a Curie point near 350°C. section_candidates.excerpt: Introduction The Waterberg Group is a thick Proterozoic sedimentary succession deposited on Archean and Paleoproterozoic rocks of the Kaapvaal Craton (Figure 1), including the ~2.06 Ga Bushveld Complex (Walraven and Hattingh, 1993; Walraven, 1997; de Waal and Armstrong, 2000; Buick et al. , 2001; Eglington and Armstrong, 2004). Rb–Sr and U–Pb dates of ~1.4 to ~1.3 Ga for the Pilanesberg Dyke Swarm and syenite of the Leeuwfontein complex that intrude parts of the group have generally been inferred to provide a younger age limit for the group (e.g. Jansen, 1982; Tankard et al., 1982; Walraven et al., 1990; Emerman, 1991). Widespread dolerite sills that intrude the Waterberg Group and predate Jurassic Karoo magmatism have common

matism in southern Africa and place tighter age constraints on the Waterberg Group than previously available. In South Africa, ~1.88 Ga dolerite intrudes upper Waterberg strata, constraining most, if not all, of the succession to have accumulated between ~2.06 Ga (age of the underlying Bushveld Complex) and ~1.88 Ga. This is consistent with derivation of much of the group from uplifted sources in reactivated segments of the Limpopo Belt. The dolerites are typical continental tholeiites, but their trace-element contents discriminate t hem from dolerite sills of the 1.1 Ga Umkondo Igneous Province, which occur in the same region. Paleomagnetic samples from dolerite intrusions in the Waterberg Group in South Africa (including one sill with a U–Pb baddeleyite age of ~1872 Ma), and from dolerite sills and basalt flows in the Soutpansberg Group to the east-northeast, yield antipodal directions with a site mean pole at 15.6°north, 17.1°east, A 95 = 8.9°. These data are interpreted to indicate that the ~1879 to ~1872 Ma dolerites were intruded into the Waterberg Group during voluminous magmatism associated with development of the Soutpansberg rift basin. Paleomagnetic data for the ~1879 to ~1872 Ma intrusions yield a new Paleoproterozoic pole for the Kaapvaal Craton, and comparisons between the ~1927 and ~1879 to ~1872 Ma post- Waterberg dolerites and broadly coeval mafic rocks elsewhere in South Africa and Zimbabwe help to constrain the nature and temporal and spatial distribution of intraplate Paleoproterozoic magmatism in the region. (1991), van der Neut et al. (1991) and Callaghan (1993). Across the Waterberg plateau and adjacent areas (Figures 2 and 3), the group has a composite stratigraphic thickness of as much as 7km. section_candidates.excerpt: Introduction The Waterberg Group is a thick Proterozoic sedimentary succession deposited on Archean and Paleoproterozoic rocks of the Kaapvaal Craton (Figure 1), including the ~2.06 Ga Bushveld Complex (Walraven and Hattingh, 1993; Walraven, 1997; de Waal and Armstrong, 2000; Buick et al. , 2001; Eglington and Armstrong, 2004). Rb–Sr and U–Pb dates of ~1.4 to ~1.3 Ga for the Pilanesberg Dyke Swarm and syenite of the Leeuwfontein complex that intrude parts of the group have generally been inferred to provide a younger age limit for the group (e.g. Jansen, 1982; Tankard et al., 1982; Walraven et al., 1990; Emerman, 1991). Widespread dolerite sills that intrude the Waterberg Group and predate Jurassic Karoo magmatism have common

matism in southern Africa and place tighter age constraints on the Waterberg Group than previously available. In South Africa, ~1.88 Ga dolerite intrudes upper Waterberg strata, constraining most, if not all, of the succession to have accumulated between ~2.06 Ga (age of the underlying Bushveld Complex) and ~1.88 Ga. This is consistent with derivation of much of the group from uplifted sources in reactivated segments of the Limpopo Belt. The dolerites are typical continental tholeiites, but their trace-element contents discriminate t hem from dolerite sills of the 1.1 Ga Umkondo Igneous Province, which occur in the same region. Paleomagnetic samples from dolerite intrusions in the Waterberg Group in South Africa (including one sill with a U–Pb baddeleyite age of ~1872 Ma), and from dolerite sills and basalt flows in the Soutpansberg Group to the east-northeast, yield antipodal directions with a site mean pole at 15.6°north, 17.1°east, A 95 = 8.9°. These data are interpreted to indicate that the ~1879 to ~1872 Ma dolerites were intruded into the Waterberg Group during voluminous magmatism associated with development of the Soutpansberg rift basin. Older, ~1927 Ma dolerite in Botswana is similar in age and geochemistry to basalts in the craton-margin Olifantshoek Supergroup, suggesting t

Tectonics Special Research Cent re, School of Earth and Geographical Sciences, The University of Western Australia, Crawley, W A 6009, Australia Correspondence should be addresse d to Zhang Shihong (e-mail: shzhang@cugb.edu.cn) Abstract A paleomagnetic study was carried out on the Yangzhuang Formation (~1350 Ma) of the Jixian System in the North China Block (NCB). Detailed stepwise thermal demagnetization isolated two components. The soft compo- nent (component A) was interpreted as a remagnetization in the recent geomagnetic field. The hard component (compo- nent B) with higher unblocking-temperatures was carried by hematite. Its site-mean direction is D/I = 77.6°/-24.3° (κ = 5.4, α95 = 18.3°, N = 15 sites) before, and D/I = 72.2°/11.5° ( κ = 24.6, α95 = 7.9°) after tilt correction. It passes a fold test (Mesozoic folding) at 99% confidence level and reversal test at 95% confidence level. The corresponding pole locates at 17.3°N, 214.5°E (dp = 4.1°, dm = 8.0°). A best fit of paleo- magnetic poles from the NCB, Baltica, Siberia and the ap- parent polar wander path for Laurentia suggests a long-lived connection between these pale o-continents between ~1800 and 1350 Ma. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: ructions between the North China Block (NCB) and other continents have been debated over a decade [1⚷6], partly due to the sparsity of reliable paleomagnetic poles from these continents for the Precambrian time. The Preca mbrian successions (ca. 1800⚷800 Ma) in the Jixian County in North China are well exposed with several reddish carbonate intervals that are suitable for paleomagnetic study. Although a number of paleomagnetic investigations have been carried out previously on these successions[7Ē9], the reliability of most earlier results is questionable due to one or more of the following reasons: unrecognized Mesozoic magnetic overprint, insufficient sampling, and lack of modern de- magnetization and field test. In this paper, we report a stable magnetic component from purple muddy dolomites in the Yangzhuang Formation (ca. 1350 Ma) that is inter- preted as a primary remanence, and discuss possible links between the NCB and other continents. 1 Regional geology and sampling In the NCB, the Mesoproterozoic to Neoproterozoic stratotype section is located at northern Jixian County, ca. 100 km east of Beijing (Fig. 1(a) ). The strata in this area consist of 10 km-thick unmetamorphosed section of clas- tic and carbonate rocks and are divided into three systems: the Changchengian (ca. 1800 ⚷1400 Ma), the Jianxianian (ca. 1400 ⚷1000 Ma) and the Qingbaikouan (ca. 1000⚷ 800 Ma). The rocks investigated in this study are characterized by the low anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility, by the absence of any predominant directions of the half-axes of the ellipsoids of anisotropy, and by the planar type of the latter. Sixty-two oriented samples from 13 sites were submitted to standard stepwise demagnetization procedures yielding a characteristic remanence carried by hematite. In order to provide new constraints on them, a paleomagnetic study was carried out on the Ediacaran succession of red claystones exposed in Sierra de los Barrientos (37.8 ◦S, 59.0◦W), Buenos Aires province, Argentina. This succesion belongs to the late Proterozoic–early Paleozoic sedimentary cover of the Rio de la Plata craton. Sixty-two oriented samples from 13 sites were submitted to standard stepwise demagnetization procedures yielding a characteristic remanence carried by hematite. A primary origin for the remanence is suggested by the apparent recording of secular variation along the stratigraphic column including a reversal of the earth magnetic ﬁeld and an improvement in clustering of mean site directions after application of bedding corrections, although the latter is not statistically signiﬁcant. , in Northeast Brazil, and its African counterparts in Nigeria and Hoggar typify the tectonic evolution of the collisional belts encircling the São Francisco craton [13–15]. Never- theless, the margins of Kalahari, Rio de la Plata and Amazon cratons, as well as the southern border of the São Francisco craton, record much younger collision events, ageing up to Cambrian times ( Fig. 1 a). In spite of their similar ages all over South America, these Cambrian events are usually viewed as of local extent. They have been named Buzius Orogeny in southeast- ern Brazil [10], and Pampean Orogeny in western Argentina [16]. Paleomagnetism provides key information to con- strain such a complex assembly history. However, the scarcity of paleomagnetic data for late Neoproterozoic and Cambrian rocks in the West Gondwana has prevented testing these geodynamic scenarios (for a review, see [17]). Here we present a high-quality paleomagnetic pole obtained on the Early Cambrian mafic dikes of Itabaiana, Paraíba State, NE Brazil. These results are then compared with data from Gondwana, Laurentia and with poles recently obtained for the Amazon craton [18]. Introduction The assembly of Gondwana is now viewed as a long-standing protracted process that may encompass most of the Neoprotero- zoic era (e.g., Meert, 2003; Trindade et al., 2006; Vaughan and Pankhurst, 2008). However, reconstructing the paleogeography of this supercontinent in its early stages is a challenging prospect, so far impeded by the scarcity of relevant well-dated paleopoles in almost all cratonic units involved. The Congo craton, a central piece of the Gondwana jigsaw-puzzle, counts only 10 Proterozoic pale- opoles between 1300 and 550 Ma (Tohver et al., 2006). These poles mainly belong to two age groups: an older one (800–700 Ma) show- ing the rapid drift of Congo before the Panafrican orogenic events, and a younger one (550–500 Ma) corresponding to the time of ﬁnal assembly of Gondwana elements. Min- eral 40Ar/39Ar ages on phlogopite separates from the kimberlite yield a mean age of 1073.5± 13.7 Ma (2σ). Paleomagnetic samples from the brecciated kimberlite yielded a mean direction with a declination of 45.3◦ and an inclination of−25.1◦ (k = 37,α95 = 9.3◦). Paleomagnetism A total of 56 sites located in Rajasthan and the Son Valley of India were sampled for paleomagnetic study using a water-cooled portable drill. Sample collection covered the sandstones and car- bonates of the Bhander and Rewa Groups. Sample orientation was performed in the ﬁeld using Brunton magnetic compasses, and solar readings were used to correct any magnetic deﬂections and local declination deviations. The samples were cut into cylindrical specimens of relatively uniform volume in the laboratory. Sam- ple susceptibility was measured on the Sapphire Instruments SI-3B Bridge, and Curie temperature runs were performed incrementally on rock powders in a KLY-3S susceptibility bridge attached to a CS-3 heating unit. Isothermal remnant magnetizations (IRM) were conducted on an ASC Scientiﬁc Model IM-10–30 impulse magne- tizer. Pilot samples were selected for preliminary demagnetization and a sequence of demagnetization steps was chosen based on these preliminary results. Sandstone samples were treated with stepwise thermal demagnetization. Magnetite bearing limestone samples were treated with initial low temperature treatments in the form of liquid N 2 baths (Dunlop and Argyle, 1991), followed by alternating ﬁelds up to 10–30 mT and stepwi

ge attached to a CS-3 heating unit. Isothermal remnant magnetizations (IRM) were conducted on an ASC Scientiﬁc Model IM-10–30 impulse magne- tizer. Pilot samples were selected for preliminary demagnetization and a sequence of demagnetization steps was chosen based on these preliminary results. Sandstone samples were treated with stepwise thermal demagnetization. Magnetite bearing limestone samples were treated with initial low temperature treatments in the form of liquid N 2 baths (Dunlop and Argyle, 1991), followed by alternating ﬁelds up to 10–30 mT and stepwise thermal demag- netization or by conventional alternating ﬁeld (AF) treatments. Thermal demagnetization was carried out using an ASC TD-48 thermal demagnetizer and AF demagnetization treatments used a DTech 2000 AF demagnetizer. All rights reserved. 1. Introduction The cratonic blocks of East Gondwana represent an important element of Proterozoic paleogeographic reconstructions and tec- tonic studies. Included in these cratonic blocks are the Rayner and Mawson cratonic blocks (East Antarctica), Australia, Mada- gascar, the Seychelles, Sri Lanka and India ( Meert, 2003; Powell and Pisarevsky, 2002 ). Further research into the age of the Lower Vindhyan sediments yielded robust Paleoproterozoic- Mesooproterozoic ages ( Ray et al., 2002; Rasmussen et al., 2002a ) and makes a Neoproterozoic–Cambrian age for the Chorhat sand- stone untenable. However, recent work hints at the possibility that Ediacaran-like fossils may be present in the lower Vindhyan basin extending complex life (though not speciﬁcally Ediacarans) into the Paleoproterozoic ( Bengtson et al., 2007 ). These incidents under- score the need for independent veriﬁcation of Vindhyan fossil ﬁnds if major conclusions are to be drawn from them. We present new palaeomagnetic data from the 616 ± 3M a (U-Pb) Egersund dykes in SW Norway, which yield a palaeolatitude of 53 ◦ +16◦/−13◦ for the studied location. This would indicate that the Baltica plate spanned latitudes between 50 ◦ and 75 ◦ Si n the Early Ediacaran. The pole position (31 ◦N, 44◦E, dp/dm = 15/17) conﬁrms earlier studies, but the primary nature of the remanence is now supported by two positive contact tests. A new 40Ar/39Ar biotite age of 600 ± 10 Ma from one of the dykes suggests that remanence acquisition in the dykes took place between 600 and 616 Ma. Thermal demagnetization results and rock magnetic experiments reveal the presence of two discrete magnetizations in UMG rocks. Both magnetizations are carried by hematite. The dominant characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) is an east-directed (or antipode) shallow, positive to negative inclination magnetization that is typically unblocked over a narrow range of high laboratory temperatures between 660 and 680 ◦C. The second magnetization, exclusively of normal polarity, is north to northeast-directed and has a moderate to steep, positive inclination and probably represents a recent or modern day viscous remanent magnetization. Because the UMG is one of the few sedimentary succes- sions associated with the incipient dispersal of Rodinia, and because of the excellent preservation of this suc- cession (i.e., lack of burial metamorphism) it provides an ideal focus for detailed paleomagnetic study. thin the UMG have been interpreted as dominantly ﬂuvial basin deposits with a source to the east and north ( Hansen, 1965; Sanderson, 1984; Sanderson and Wiley, 1986; Farmer and Ball, 1997) or a mixed ﬂuvial-marine environment ( Wallace and Crittenden, 1969; Wallace, 1972; Dehler et al., 2006). Detailed sedimentologic and stratigraphic stud- ies are warranted to resolve questions about depositional environments, paleogeography, and basin type. The UMG ranges in thickness from 4 km in the west to over 7 km in the east (Link et al., 1993). The western UMG is composed of quartzose and arkosic sandstone and interbedded mudstone, much of which is hematite- cemented. The eastern section consists of conglomerate, sandstone and mudstone, and most sandstone units in the east are hematite-cemented redbeds (Hansen, 1965). The UMG nonconformably overlies the Red Creek Quartzite and Owiyukuts Complex (∼1.7–∼2.7 Ga,Hansen, 1965; Sears et al., 1982 ). Methods Twelve sampling localities were established in UMG rocks. These include seven localities in the eastern Uintas (Home Mountain Canyon, Irish Canyon, Bull Canyon, Sparks, Lone Mountain, Cross Mountain, and Juniper Mountain) and, ﬁve localities in the north-central Uin- tas (Sheep Creek Canyon, Browne Lake, Carter Creek, Dowd Springs, and Flaming Gorge Reservoir dam) (Fig. 2). The localities were selected based on exposure of continuous and thick sections of strata. Sampling was focused on hematite-cemented medium to ﬁne-grained sandstone and siltstone. Each site was deﬁned by an individual stratigraphic bed, or several successive beds, and 7–12 independently oriented samples were obtained. With a growing body of information sup- porting periods of exceedingly unusual climate behavior for Earth in the Neoproterozoic, additional, robust pale- omagnetic data for this time period have become even more important. Some initial paleomagnetic data from mid-Neoproterozoic rocks from North America (e.g., Park and Aitken, 1986; Elston, 1993; Park et al., 1995; Weil et al., 2003, 2004) are consistent with the possibil- ity of North America lying at or near the equator during this time period, but some of these data sets are of limited quality and their overall reliability is open to question. To better understand the drift history and the APWP of Laurentia for the latest Neoproterozoic, we have under- taken a comprehensive paleomagnetic study of the Neo- proterozoic Uinta Mountain Group (UMG), northeast Utah, northwest Colorado, and southwest Wyoming. The UMG is one of the thickest and best preserved Neopro- terozoic sedimentary rock successions in North America. Because the UMG is one of the few sedimentary succes- sions associated with the incipient dispersal of Rodinia, and because of the excellent preservation of this suc- cession (i.e., lack of burial metamorphism) it provides an ideal focus for detailed paleomagnetic study. Isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) acqui- sition and backﬁeld demagnetization experiments, using a pulse DC magnet capable of ﬁelds of 3.2 T, were per- formed on selected samples from all localities to further evaluate the magnetic mineralogy. Three-axis IRM ther- mal demagnetization experiments ( Lowrie, 1990) were performed using three DC ﬁelds (3.0, 0.3, and 0.03 T; or “hard,” “medium” and “soft,” respectively) along three orthogonal axes. Remanence directions were calculated from princi- pal component analysis ( Kirschvink, 1980 ) of linear vectors picked from orthogonal projection demagneti- zation plots (Zijderveld, 1967). Estimated directions for specimens were accepted for site mean determinations if unanchored maximum angular deviation (MAD) val- ues were less than 15 ◦. Specimens that could not be resolved to MADs of less than 15 ◦, as well as those specimens with anomalous directions (i.e., individual direction greater than two angular standard deviations from the estimated mean) were rejected for site mean calculations. thin the UMG have been interpreted as dominantly ﬂuvial basin deposits with a source to the east and north ( Hansen, 1965; Sanderson, 1984; Sanderson and Wiley, 1986; Farmer and Ball, 1997) or a mixed ﬂuvial-marine environment ( Wallace and Crittenden, 1969; Wallace, 1972; Dehler et al., 2006). Detailed sedimentologic and stratigraphic stud- ies are warranted to resolve questions about depositional environments, paleogeography, and basin type. The UMG ranges in thickness from 4 km in the west to over 7 km in the east (Link et al., 1993). The western UMG is composed of quartzose and arkosic sandstone and interbedded mudstone, much of which is hematite- cemented. The eastern section consists of conglomerate, sandstone and mudstone, and most sandstone units in the east are hematite-cemented redbeds (Hansen, 1965). The UMG nonconformably overlies the Red Creek Quartzite and Owiyukuts Complex (∼1.7–∼2.7 Ga,Hansen, 1965; Sears et al., 1982 ). The Red Creek Quartzite and Owiyukuts Complex are composed of metaquartzite, amphibolite and mica schist ( Schell, 1969; Sears et al., 1982; Hansen, 1984 ) and are restricted to the struc- turally high, northeastern region of the Uinta Mountains. Rock magnetism and magnetic mineralogy, UMG Rocks Thermal demagnetization of all UMG rocks inves- tigated reveals that hematite is the primary carrier of what we interpret as an ancient, primary to near primary Neoproterozoic magnetization as well as the secondary magnetization that is pervasive at many UMG localities. High laboratory unblocking temperatures were observed for almost all of the samples, with most unblocking between about 600 ◦ and 670 ◦C. However, NRM intensi- ties show less of a correlation with the presence of a speciﬁc magnetization. In general, histograms of NRM intensities for specimens dominated by a secondary mag- netization show median values that are up to an order of magnitude greater than those of specimens that contain only the east or west-directed and shallow magnetiza- tion. Chemical demagnetization of NRM (Figs. 3b and c and 4b–f) shows that ﬁne-grained, pigmentary hematite is the principal form of hematite present in all UMG rocks. With a growing body of information sup- porting periods of exceedingly unusual climate behavior for Earth in the Neoproterozoic, additional, robust pale- omagnetic data for this time period have become even more important. Some initial paleomagnetic data from mid-Neoproterozoic rocks from North America (e.g., Park and Aitken, 1986; Elston, 1993; Park et al., 1995; Weil et al., 2003, 2004) are consistent with the possibil- ity of North America lying at or near the equator during this time period, but some of these data sets are of limited quality and their overall reliability is open to question. To better understand the drift history and the APWP of Laurentia for the latest Neoproterozoic, we have under- taken a comprehensive paleomagnetic study of the Neo- proterozoic Uinta Mountain Group (UMG), northeast Utah, northwest Colorado, and southwest Wyoming. The UMG is one of the thickest and best preserved Neopro- terozoic sedimentary rock successions in North America. Because the UMG is one of the few sedimentary succes- sions associated with the incipient dispersal of Rodinia, and because of the excellent preservation of this suc- cession (i.e., lack of burial metamorphism) it provides an ideal focus for detailed paleomagnetic study. Sampling was focused on hematite-cemented medium to ﬁne-grained sandstone and siltstone. Each site was deﬁned by an individual stratigraphic bed, or several successive beds, and 7–12 independently oriented samples were obtained. A total of 195 sites from 12 localities were collected in UMG strata. Natural remanent magnetization (NRM) data were obtained using superconducting rock magnetometers in magnetically shielded rooms at the University of New Mexico and at the University of Michigan. Stepwise demagnetization was performed to determine the direc- tion of characteristic remanent magnetizations (ChRM). For all UMG rocks, both thermal and chemical demag- netization, using reagent grade hydrochloric acid at room temperature ( Henry, 1979), were used to effec- tively isolate ChRMs. Chemical demagnetization was performed in a low ﬁeld space ( H ∼200 nT) in a fume hood. Isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) acqui- sition and backﬁeld demagnetization experiments, using a pulse DC magnet capable of ﬁelds of 3.2 T, were per- formed on selected samples from all localities to further evaluate the magnetic mineralogy. Isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) acqui- sition and backﬁeld demagnetization experiments, using a pulse DC magnet capable of ﬁelds of 3.2 T, were per- formed on selected samples from all localities to further evaluate the magnetic mineralogy. Three-axis IRM ther- mal demagnetization experiments ( Lowrie, 1990) were performed using three DC ﬁelds (3.0, 0.3, and 0.03 T; or “hard,” “medium” and “soft,” respectively) along three orthogonal axes. Remanence directions were calculated from princi- pal component analysis ( Kirschvink, 1980 ) of linear vectors picked from orthogonal projection demagneti- zation plots (Zijderveld, 1967). Estimated directions for specimens were accepted for site mean determinations if unanchored maximum angular deviation (MAD) val- ues were less than 15 ◦. Specimens that could not be resolved to MADs of less than 15 ◦, as well as those specimens with anomalous directions (i.e., individual direction greater than two angular standard deviations from the estimated mean) were rejected for site mean calculations. With a growing body of information sup- porting periods of exceedingly unusual climate behavior for Earth in the Neoproterozoic, additional, robust pale- omagnetic data for this time period have become even more important. Some initial paleomagnetic data from mid-Neoproterozoic rocks from North America (e.g., Park and Aitken, 1986; Elston, 1993; Park et al., 1995; Weil et al., 2003, 2004) are consistent with the possibil- ity of North America lying at or near the equator during this time period, but some of these data sets are of limited quality and their overall reliability is open to question. To better understand the drift history and the APWP of Laurentia for the latest Neoproterozoic, we have under- taken a comprehensive paleomagnetic study of the Neo- proterozoic Uinta Mountain Group (UMG), northeast Utah, northwest Colorado, and southwest Wyoming. The UMG is one of the thickest and best preserved Neopro- terozoic sedimentary rock successions in North America. Because the UMG is one of the few sedimentary succes- sions associated with the incipient dispersal of Rodinia, and because of the excellent preservation of this suc- cession (i.e., lack of burial metamorphism) it provides an ideal focus for detailed paleomagnetic study. thin the UMG have been interpreted as dominantly ﬂuvial basin deposits with a source to the east and north ( Hansen, 1965; Sanderson, 1984; Sanderson and Wiley, 1986; Farmer and Ball, 1997) or a mixed ﬂuvial-marine environment ( Wallace and Crittenden, 1969; Wallace, 1972; Dehler et al., 2006). Detailed sedimentologic and stratigraphic stud- ies are warranted to resolve questions about depositional environments, paleogeography, and basin type. The UMG ranges in thickness from 4 km in the west to over 7 km in the east (Link et al., 1993). The western UMG is composed of quartzose and arkosic sandstone and interbedded mudstone, much of which is hematite- cemented. The eastern section consists of conglomerate, sandstone and mudstone, and most sandstone units in the east are hematite-cemented redbeds (Hansen, 1965). The UMG nonconformably overlies the Red Creek Quartzite and Owiyukuts Complex (∼1.7–∼2.7 Ga,Hansen, 1965; Sears et al., 1982 ). Methods Twelve sampling localities were established in UMG rocks. These include seven localities in the eastern Uintas (Home Mountain Canyon, Irish Canyon, Bull Canyon, Sparks, Lone Mountain, Cross Mountain, and Juniper Mountain) and, ﬁve localities in the north-central Uin- tas (Sheep Creek Canyon, Browne Lake, Carter Creek, Dowd Springs, and Flaming Gorge Reservoir dam) (Fig. 2). With a growing body of information sup- porting periods of exceedingly unusual climate behavior for Earth in the Neoproterozoic, additional, robust pale- omagnetic data for this time period have become even more important. Some initial paleomagnetic data from mid-Neoproterozoic rocks from North America (e.g., Park and Aitken, 1986; Elston, 1993; Park et al., 1995; Weil et al., 2003, 2004) are consistent with the possibil- ity of North America lying at or near the equator during this time period, but some of these data sets are of limited quality and their overall reliability is open to question. To better understand the drift history and the APWP of Laurentia for the latest Neoproterozoic, we have under- taken a comprehensive paleomagnetic study of the Neo- proterozoic Uinta Mountain Group (UMG), northeast Utah, northwest Colorado, and southwest Wyoming. The UMG is one of the thickest and best preserved Neopro- terozoic sedimentary rock successions in North America. Because the UMG is one of the few sedimentary succes- sions associated with the incipient dispersal of Rodinia, and because of the excellent preservation of this suc- cession (i.e., lack of burial metamorphism) it provides an ideal focus for detailed paleomagnetic study. Some initial paleomagnetic data from mid-Neoproterozoic rocks from North America (e.g., Park and Aitken, 1986; Elston, 1993; Park et al., 1995; Weil et al., 2003, 2004) are consistent with the possibil- ity of North America lying at or near the equator during this time period, but some of these data sets are of limited quality and their overall reliability is open to question. Because the UMG is one of the few sedimentary succes- sions associated with the incipient dispersal of Rodinia, and because of the excellent preservation of this suc- cession (i.e., lack of burial metamorphism) it provides an ideal focus for detailed paleomagnetic study. e ﬁne- to medium-grained ( ≤1 to 2 mm average grain size) diabase. They consist of clinopyroxene (augite) and plagioclase, with minor biotite and amphibole. Maﬁc minerals are slightly altered to chlorite, and plagioclase is saussuritized. These dikes are ophitic and subophitic to intergranular; porphyritic and glom- eroporphyritic textures are sometimes present. Group A dikes are thin, with thicknesses ranging from 2 to 7 m. The dikes are chemically undifferentiated, display moderate iron-enrichment, and are among the most primitive of the dikes in the southern Tobacco Root Mountains (Wooden et al., 1978). Evidence for such a remagnetiza- tion is compelling along the Mammoth fault in the northern Tobacco Root Mountains where a Laramide thrust fault intensely sheared and fractured the Mammoth diabase dike (Fig. 2B). The fault controlled the emplacement of the Tobacco Root Batholith (Schmidt et al., 1990 ) and acted as a conduit for late stage magmatic ﬂuids or ﬂuids associated with subsequent precious mineralization. Evidence for ﬂuid activity includes extensive chloritization and epidotization of the dike, and locally intense siliciﬁcation. The remanence may have been caused by growth of secondary magnetite around original titanomagnetite grains, by growth of new magnetite by precipitation of iron during for- mation of secondary alteration phases, or by a combination of both processes. Some magnetite may also have formed during oxidation of magmatic sulﬁdes present within the dike. It is unlikely to be the result of widespread tectonothermal activity with temperatures greater than 300 ◦C given the preservation of Proterozoic ages from biotites in basement rocks from the southern Tobacco Root Mountains, including the biotite from the baked contact zone at site TR50 described above. Evidence for such a remagnetiza- tion is compelling along the Mammoth fault in the northern Tobacco Root Mountains where a Laramide thrust fault intensely sheared and fractured the Mammoth diabase dike (Fig. 2B). The fault controlled the emplacement of the Tobacco Root Batholith (Schmidt et al., 1990 ) and acted as a conduit for late stage magmatic ﬂuids or ﬂuids associated with subsequent precious mineralization. Evidence for ﬂuid activity includes extensive chloritization and epidotization of the dike, and locally intense siliciﬁcation. The remanence may have been caused by growth of secondary magnetite around original titanomagnetite grains, by growth of new magnetite by precipitation of iron during for- mation of secondary alteration phases, or by a combination of both processes. Some magnetite may also have formed during oxidation of magmatic sulﬁdes present within the dike. This period has also been proposed to host unusual geodynamic events such as rapid plate motions and/or the bulk tumbling of the Earth with respect to its spin axis, called true polar wander (TPW). New paleomagnetic and 40Ar–39Ar geochronologic results have been obtained from a pair of shallowly emplaced syenitic intrusions in western Quebec. The Mont Rigaud and the Chatham-Grenville stocks are related to a failed rift arm of the Iapetus Ocean. The position of Baltica within the circum-Iapetus paleogeography is contentious, due to differing interpretations of the few paleomagnetic results. During Ediacaran time, Laurentia underwent large apparent polar wander that is manifested as motion from low latitude at 615 Ma to the south polar region at 590–575 Ma, and then rapidly back to low latitude by 565–550 Ma. This period has also been proposed to host unusual geodynamic events such as rapid plate motions and/or the bulk tumbling of the Earth with respect to its spin axis, called true polar wander (TPW). New paleomagnetic and 40Ar–39Ar geochronologic results have been obtained from a pair of shallowly emplaced syenitic intrusions in western Quebec. The Mont Rigaud and the Chatham-Grenville stocks are related to a failed rift arm of the Iapetus Ocean. Both intrusions bear hornblendes which provide overlapping 40Ar–39Ar plateau ages of 533.2 ± 1.1 Ma (Mont Rigaud) and 531.4 ± 3.4 Ma (Chatham-Grenville), corresponding to Early Cambrian (Nemakit-Daldynian) time. Characteristic paleomagnetic (reversed) directions from both intrusions are easterly and shallow (D = 89.3◦, I = 30.1◦; α95 = 6.2, k = 38.8; N = 15 sites), and the Mont Rigaud intrusion also carries antipodal normal-polarity directions. The combined result yields a north

occurred at ca. 615 Ma followed by late-stage alka- lic volcanism prior to the Early Cambrian onset of Iapetan seaﬂoor-spreading ( Kumarapeli, 1993; Bingen et al., 1998; Puffer, 2002 ). An earliest Cambrian rift- to-drift transition is inferred from Cambro-Ordovician subsidence curves that are derived from the pas- sive margin successions of western Newfoundland and the central Appalachians ( Bond et al., 1984 ). A widespread carbonate platform and archaeocyathan reefs of Atdabanian age in the Forteau Forma- tion of southeastern Labrador further indicate that a warm-water passive margin had been established by mid-Early Cambrian time ( Williams and Hiscott, 1987). For this work, two rift-related intrusions have been sampled for paleomagnetic and 40Ar–39Ar geochrono- logic study. The Mont Rigaud and Chatham-Grenville stocks are a pair of silica-saturated syenitic–granitic intrusions west of Montreal ( Figs. 1 and 2 ). The intru- sions are emplaced in the craton adjacent to or within the Ottawa-Bonnechere aulacogen, and have not undergone signiﬁcant post-emplacement tilting ( Philpotts, 1976; Malka et al., 2000 ). Hand-picked separates of horn- blende and potassium feldspar grains were rinsed with deionized water and dried. Single, non-aggregate grains of 1–2 mm size were then selected under a binocular microscope for further analysis. Several grains from each site were packaged at the University of Michigan Radio- genic Isotope Geochemistry Laboratory in an aluminum foil capsule and irradiated for 300 h at the Phoenix-Ford Memorial Reactor at the University of Michigan. Neu- tron ﬂux gradients were monitored using the MMhb-1 standard (520.4 Ma; Samson and Alexander, 1987). During analysis, single grains were step-heated until fusion by an automated argon-ion laser which was defocused to ensure uniform heating. Individual steps consisted of 60 s heating followed by 2 min of gas puriﬁ- cation using two 10 1/s SAES getters (ST101 alloy) and a liquid N 2 cold ﬁnger to remove the active gasses prior to mass spectrometry. Argon isotopic ratios were measured with a VG1200S mass spectrometer. Extraction line blanks were run after every six steps. Duplicate grains were analysed to assess grain-to-grain variability and the reproducibility of the results. The 40Ar–39Ar plateau ages given below are

Horn- blende grains at site CG13 of the Chatham-Grenville stock either do not yield a stable plateau or appear to be compromised by the degassing of pyroxene with the hornblende, thus leading us to exclude site 13 from the overall age estimate. The remaining three sample sites MR10, CG31 and CG14 ( Fig. 2 ) provide an overall hornblende 40Ar–39Ar age of 531.9± 1.4 Ma (weighted mean of the ﬁve hornblende plateau ages). The potassium feldspar age data from all four sam- ple sites record 39Ar loss at some point in their history; all analysed potassium feldspars exhibit an apparent age minima at ∼5–25% degassed 39Ar, followed by a “stair- case” degassing spectrum of increasing apparent age. The feldspars B86a and B86b from site CG31 ( Fig. 3e) may be considered the least disturbed of those analysed, having the least prominent minimum apparent age (of ca. 460 Ma) and latter step ages that approach the horn- blende age from the site, as well as total gas ages of ca. 535 Ma. Overall, the potassium feldspars from the two stocks are most simply interpreted as having initially closed in the early Paleozoic, if not in the Early Cam- brian itself, with a subsequent reheating event having caused variable 39Ar loss. Laurentia likely resided at low southerly paleolatitudes throughout the Cambrian, ruling out a major inertial-interchange TPW event for Early to Middle Cambrian time. A comparison of Late Ediacaran to Middle Cambrian paleomagnetic results from Laurentia, Baltica, Siberia and elements of West Gondwana implies that by Early Cambrian time a large paleolatitudinal gap existed between Laurentia and its presumed conjugate rift margins, thus placing a wide Iapetus Ocean between them. The position of Baltica within the circum-Iapetus paleogeography is contentious, due to differing interpretations of the few paleomagnetic results. During Ediacaran time, Laurentia underwent large apparent polar wander that is manifested as motion from low latitude at 615 Ma to the south polar region at 590–575 Ma, and then rapidly back to low latitude by 565–550 Ma. These rapid apparent motions complicate attempts to reconstruct the paleogeography, and have led to non-uniformitarian proposals such as rapid plate motion during the terminal Neoproterozoic opening of the Iapetus (McCausland and Hodych, 1998; Cawood et al., 2001 ) or the contribution of substantial true polar wander (TPW) during the Early Cambrian (Kirschvink et al., 1997; Evans, 1998). This study provides new hornblende and potassium feldspar 40Ar–39Ar age dating and primary paleomag- netic results for the Mont Rigaud and Chatham-Grenville stocks of western Quebec. The paleomagnetic results apply to Laurentia for Early Cambrian time, a period which is not well represented for Laurentia. The 40Ar–39Ar ages also extend the region of recognized Early Cambrian rift-related magmatism of Laurentia’s Iapetan margin to include the northeastern Laurentia, conﬁrming that rift-related activity took place there for ca. 80 myears during Ediacaran to Early Cambrian time. 2. Paleomagnetism The Mont Rigaud and Chatham-Grenville stocks were sampled by portable gas-powered drill and as ori- ented hand-samples. Both methods produced standard 2.54 cm diameter core samples, and each paleomagnetic site consisted typically of six samples. The Mont Rigaud stock and environs were sampled in 27 sites, providing 320 standard 2.2 cm length specimens for analysis and the Chatham-Grenville stock and environs were sampled in 31 sites, providing 305 specimens. The specimens underwent thermal and alternating ﬁeld (AF) stepwise demagnetization at the University of Michigan using a Sapphire Instruments SI-4 AF demag- netizer, an ASC TD-48 thermal demagnetizer, and a 2G cryogenic magnetometer, all set inside a magnetically shielded room which permits entry of only∼0.2% of the Earth’s ambient magnetic ﬁeld intensity. The position of Baltica within the circum-Iapetus paleogeography is contentious, due to differing interpretations of the few paleomagnetic results. During Ediacaran time, Laurentia underwent large apparent polar wander that is manifested as motion from low latitude at 615 Ma to the south polar region at 590–575 Ma, and then rapidly back to low latitude by 565–550 Ma. These rapid apparent motions complicate attempts to reconstruct the paleogeography, and have led to non-uniformitarian proposals such as rapid plate motion during the terminal Neoproterozoic opening of the Iapetus (McCausland and Hodych, 1998; Cawood et al., 2001 ) or the contribution of substantial true polar wander (TPW) during the Early Cambrian (Kirschvink et al., 1997; Evans, 1998). This study provides new hornblende and potassium feldspar 40Ar–39Ar age dating and primary paleomag- netic results for the Mont Rigaud and Chatham-Grenville stocks of western Quebec. The paleomagnetic results apply to Laurentia for Early Cambrian time, a period which is not well represented for Laurentia. The 40Ar–39Ar ages also extend the region of recognized Early Cambrian rift-related magmatism of Laurentia’s Iapetan margin to include the northeastern Laurentia, conﬁrming that rift-related activity took place there for ca. 80 myears during Ediacaran to Early Cambrian time. 2. Forty-eight sites of samples were collected from the Sugetbrak and Chigebrak Formations. Twenty-four sites of sandstone and volcanic rock from the Sugetbrak Formation revealed stable characteristic remanent components (ChRm) isolated between 500 and 680 ◦C. The computed magnetic directions from these components are consistent and signiﬁcantly distinguished from those of younger ages. Both normal and reverse polarities have been observed, and a positive fold test is revealed after bedding corrections at 95% conﬁdence level. Anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility measurements shows primary sedimentary fabrics with weak anisotropy degrees. A paleomagnetic pole is calculated at 19.1 ◦N, 149.7◦E, k = 11.2, A95 = 9.3◦ with n = 24, yielding a paleolatitude of∼27◦N for the sampling area. The chemo-stratigraphic correlation of this section with reference ones reveals an average age of∼595 Ma. A new paleogeographic reconstruction has been attempted showing general low paleolatitude positions for the Australia, South China and Tarim blocks at about 600 Ma. This observation provides new evidences for the snowball Earth hypothesis. © 2007 Elsevier B.V . All rights reserved. Keywords: Paleomagnetism; Aksu; Tarim

This hypothesis implies that the Earth experienced sev- eral complete freezes in its history. The three most acceptable episodes are the Sturtain, Marinoan, and Gaskiers (Hankalchough in Tarim) glaciations ( Grey and Corkeron, 1998; Xiao et al., 2004; Condon et al., 2005). Age range of the Sugetbrak F ormation Though several radiometric attempts have been made to date the basalt interlayer at the top of the Lower Sugetbrak Formation, no direct age constraint was obtained. However, a chemo-stratigraphic investigation on the same section of the Sugetbrak Formation in Area I have been carried out allowing estimating the formation age. The characteristic δ 13C curve presents two negative and two positive carbon excursions that are comparable to that of the Doushantuo Formation of South China (Fig. 7, modiﬁed after He et al., in press ). In summary, this paleomagnetic study yields a reliable paleomagnetic pole for the Neoproterozoic Sugetbrak Formation based on (1) well deﬁned and stable magnetic remanent carriers; (2) the presence of both polarities; (3) positive fold test; (4) negligible deformation demon- strated by AMS measurements; (5) consistent magnetic directions shown by both sedimentary and volcanic rocks from two distant areas. Within the same time, “the great Infra-Cambrian glaciation” slowly evolved into the snowball Earth hypothesis (Kirschvink, 1992; Hoffman et al., 1998; Hoffman and Schrag, 2002). This hypothesis implies that the Earth experienced sev- eral complete freezes in its history. The three most acceptable episodes are the Sturtain, Marinoan, and Gaskiers (Hankalchough in Tarim) glaciations ( Grey and Corkeron, 1998; Xiao et al., 2004; Condon et al., 2005). However, the existence of these low latitude global glaciations relies upon a small number of high quality paleomagnetic data, such as those from the Elatina Formation in Australia ( Schmidt and Williams, 1995; Sohl et al., 1999 ). More paleomagnetic data from the other blocks are needed to verify low lat- itude glaciations, and forwardly, to test the snowball Earth hypothesis. For this reason, and also to better constrain the paleogeography reconstructions, paleo- magnetic studies have been carried out in the Tarim basin where the Neoproterozoic glacier deposits have been well documented (Gao and Zhu, 1984; Gao et al., 1985). 2. Geological setting and paleomagnetic sampling The Aksu area is located in the northwestern part of the Tarim basin, NW China ( Fig. 1 a). The strati- graphic succession includes the Mesoproterozoic Aksu group of metamorphic rocks, the Lower Neoproterozoic Qiaoenbrak Formation, the Yuermeinak Formation, the Upper Neoproterozoic Sugetbrak Formation, the Chige- brak Formation and the Cambrian Yuertus Formation (Fig. 1 b). Continental and marine glacial deposits are observed in the Yuermeinak and Qiaoenbrak formations (Gao and Zhu, 1984; Gao et al., 1985 ; Fig. 1 b). Ter- restrial clastic, shallow marine carbonated rocks, with minor interbedded basaltic ﬂows, characterize the late Neoproterozoic strata. Introduction From its assemblage at around 550 Ma to its amalgamation with Laurussia to form Pangaea in the latest Palaeozoic, the Gondwana supercontinent seems to have wandered over the South Pole following a complex path, as suggested by the palaeomagnetic poles determined from its main constituent plates, especially Australia, Africa and South America. e Achala Batholith (31°30 ′S, 64°45 ′W, Córdoba, Argentina) is a major magmatic complex of the Sierras Pampeanas, emplaced as a post- orogenic pluton in a metamorphic –plutonic basement. It is mainly a porphyritic to coarse-grained equigranular monzogranite, with crystallization age of ∼ 370 and cooling age of ∼ 340 Ma, presently exposed as asymmetric, eastward-tilted blocks. Forty-three sites were sampled in the Achala monzogranite. Overall, it is weakly magnetic, with a mean magnetic susceptibility of 15 × 10 − 5 (SI). Twenty-two sites showed unstable magnetic behaviour. The remaining 21 sites have haematite as magnetic carrier of a stable remanence. The ilmeno-haematite appears as an accessory mineral, with exsolved intergrowths of (haemo)ilmenite. The pole better coincides with the 370 – 360 Ma segment of the Gondwana apparent polar wander path, suggesting that remanence was acquired quickly. The ﬁrst one is obtained from well-dated 1770± 12 Ma (U–Pb) gabbros and dolerites from the Ropruchey Sills whose mag- netizatizion is considered primary in origin (Fedotova et al., 1999). The second one is determined from sandstones from the top of the Shosksha Formation ( Pisarevsky and Sokolov, 2001 ). These sedi

c Province (THO) suggest high paleolatitudes for Laurentia, whereas poles from cratonic provinces (Superior, Churchill and Coronation) indicate moderate paleolatitudes. The 1830 Ma Molson dikes (Superior Craton) yield three components but the primary or secondary nature of these components is debatable ( Zhai et al., 1994; Halls and Heaman, 2000 ). (1973) obtained pale- omagnetic data for sedimentary rocks of the Kazan Formation, volcanic rocks from Christopher Island Formation (Dubawnt Group- Churchill province) besides two large dikes considered as feeding dikes of the Christopher Island lava ﬂows. All these rocks presented consistent results that passed reversal and baked contact tests. Usu- ally, dyke swarms that yield good palaeomagnetic information and are amenable to U-Pb zircon or baddelyite dating have proven to be the most useful (Buchanet al. 2000). That the remanence is primary can be demonstrated through positive contact tests (s.s.), by identify- ing secular variation between separate dykes, and by demonstrating consistent stable directions (notwithstanding secular variation) over a wide geographical area. While a fold test can constrain the timing of remanence acquisition to be prior to folding, this in itself may not be enough to invoke ‘primary’ magnetization. However, petro- graphic and rock-magnetic evidence, in addition to a positive fold test, can provide very strong evidence that the remanence dates from the time of crystallization. Received 2006 August 4; in original form 2006 April 1 SUMMARY The pole position for the late Mesoproterozoic Alcurra (formerly Kulgera) Dyke Swarm (ADS), Musgrave Block, central Australia, has been revised by adding new data from two more dykes. A palaeomagnetic fold test is positive at the 99 percent conﬁdence level and the pole position is latitude = 2.8 ◦ S, longitude= 80.4◦E( dp = 7.2◦, dm = 10.7◦). on two samples of aggregates of very ﬁne-grained biotite from the mesostasis of a Stuart Dyke (SD), Arunta Inlier, Northern Territory, yield ages of 1059± 2 and 1066 ± 3M a( 2σ ). These new ages are in agreement with those of the ∼1070 Ma Warakurna large igneous province, west-central Australia, indicating that both the ADS and SD belong to that suite. Palaeomagnetic poles determined by others for the ADS and SD are indistinguishable from each other but cannot be presently combined as a single pole because the published information on the SD is incomplete. An analysis of the palaeogeography implied by the dispersed palaeomagnetic poles from members of the extended Warakurna suite shows that the present relationships between the major Precambrian cratons (West, North and South Australian), which constitute Australia west of the Tasman Line, are inconsistent with the inferred relationship at∼1070 Ma. Nor is it apparent that internal deformations within the separate cratons are the cause of the dispersion. Our ﬁndings imply that these major Australian Cratons must have ﬁnally assembled sometime after ∼1070 Ma. n of the solid core is believed to trigger the transition of the tectonic mode from plum to plate tectonic around the Archaean– Proterozic boundary (e.g. Khain 2001). The subsequent tectonic evolution of the Earth consists mainly of the further development of plate tectonics and gradual increase of lithosphere depth (Khain 2001). Various models predict different formation times of the Earth’ s solid core. Understanding the temporal evolution of geomagnetic ﬁeld during the Archaean and Proterozic is essential to any solid- core formation model. However, the current paucity of palaeointen- sity data in the Precambrian does not allow any robust conclusions to make about the geomagnetic ﬁeld at this time. For this time pe- riod, covering almost 90 per cent of the Earth’ s history, only about 150 palaeointensity determinations have been published (these data can be found elsewhere, for example, in the world palaeoin- tensity databases http://wwwbrk.adm.yar.ru/palmag/index.html or ftp://ftp.ngdc.noaa.gov/seg/potﬁd/paleo.html). Applying only a mild selection criterion to the data drastically reduces this num- ber (Perrin & Shcherbakov 1997). Two components of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) were isolated in the sill with alternating ﬁeld and thermal treatments. The ﬁrst component is a low coercivity component of viscous origin with a direction similar to that of the Earth’s present ﬁeld at the sampling site. Anisotropy of Magnetic Susceptibility (AMS) and Structural Control [13] Bedding control is one of the major difficulties in these massive volcanic rocks. Measurements of the AMS indicate the preferred orientation of magnetic minerals, and are used here in two ways. On the one hand, it is one of the best tools to evaluate the degree of internal strain in rocks and is necessary to discard the possibility of deviations of the natural remanent magnetization [e.g., Tarling and Hrouda, 1993; Cogne´, 1987]. On the other hand, the shape and orientation of the ellipsoid of magnetic susceptibility can be regarded as an independent ind

ineation cannot correspond to the magmatic flow, as these rocks are part of a subhorizontal lava flow (K. Bull, written communication, 2003). The possibility that this vertical elongation results from horizon- tal contraction associated with the formation of jointing can also be discounted, since magnetite or a magnetite-like mineral, which probably predominantly controlled the sus- ceptibility (see rock magnetism, below), is crystallized at much higher temperature than the temperature at which columnar jointing forms. The vertical elongation must then correspond to tectonic effects. A paleomagnetic study was carried out in the well-dated Ambone and Ural volcanics in the central subprovince of Lachlan Orogen, New South Wales. Anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility measurements confirms detailed mapping of the region and shows that these massive dacitic sills and/or lava flows are flat lying. Two components of magnetization can be identified: a midtemperature direction yielding a corresponding pole in Australian coordinates l = 67.9 S/ f = 084.4 E (B = 5; n = 21; dp = 17.5 /dm = 23.1 ) and a high- temperature direction with a corresponding VGPl = 24.4 S/f = 060.6 E (B = 5; n = 25; dp = 1.4 /dm = 2.5 ). The first is interpreted as corresponding to an Early Carboniferous pole position and can be regarded as an overprint probably related to the Early Carboniferous Kanimblan orogenic event. As part of a project on the Gondwana APW path, this paper reports findings of a paleomagnetic study of rift basins in the central subprovince of the Lachlan Orogen (New South Wales) that has implications for both global paleogeography and the tectonic evolution of the orogen (Figure 2). 2. Geological Setting [5] The Lachlan Orogen is divided into several structural subprovinces, three in the models of Gray et al. [1997] and four in the models of Glen [1992, 2005]. Samples described in this paper are located in the central subprovince of the Lachlan Orogen, lying inboard (west) of relics of former intraoceanic island arc, the Macquarie V olcanic Arc (Figure 2) that formed from west dipping subduction, throughout the Ordovician [ Glen et al. , 1998, 2003; Glen, 2004; Glen et al. , 2004]. [ 6] After the Late Ordovician – Early Silurian Benambran Orogeny in which Ordovician craton-derived turbidite ter- ranes were assembled adjacent to the arc [ Glen, 2005], the plate boundary between the proto-Pacific plate and the Gondwana margin underwent major rollback back to the east. These uncertainties are due to the lack of reliable paleomagnetic data from the Gondwana continents for this key period, leading to different Apparent Polar Wander Paths (APWP) for this supercontinent (e.g. Morel and Irving, 1978; Schmidt et al., 1990; Bachtadse and Briden, 1990; V an der V oo, 1993; McElhinny et al., 2003). The African APWP for the Paleozoic times is not very well defined, especially for the Upper Devonian – Lower Carboniferous (Bachtadse et al., 1987; Aifa et al., 1990; Bachtadse and Briden, 1991; Smith et al., 1994 ). Several paleomagnetic studies carried out on Devonian and Carboniferous sedimentary rocks in the stable Saharan craton (southern Algeria) in order to improve this curve, but the results correspond rather to secondary magnetizations ( Aifa, 1993; Derder et al., 1997; Bayou et al., 2000; Henry et al., 2004a ). Because magmatic rocks often present more accurate magnetic characteristics than those obtained from sedimentary rocks, paleomagnetic investigation was carried out on doleritic rocks. The dolerites subject to this study intruded the horizontal tabular Devonian formations of the Tin Serririne basin during Lower Carboniferous times. 2. Bournas (1998) indicates these rocks as basaltic flows in his stratigraphical descrip- tion, but no evidence of flows has been observed. On the contrary, in a narrow outcrop, local symmetrical tilting around a NW –SE direction can be observed in series overlying the magmatic rocks, indicating prob- ably that the latter form here a thin dyke. Moreover, levels overlying magmatic rocks are baked or affected by hydrothermal phenomenon, showing that the basic rocks were intruded within the sedimentary formations. Anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility measurements (Djellit et al., submitted for publication ) confirmed the intrusive character of these rocks: subhorizontal magnetic foliation obtained in some sites indicates emplacement as sill but subvertical magnetic foliation on the contrary characterizes intrusion as dyke in other sites. Owing the very small difference in elevation of the host rocks under and above the sill, the latter should be thin. The fact that these sills and dykes are all located within the same level of the Lower –Middle Devonian is surprising, because this level has appar- ently similar sedimentary characteristics as the overly- ing levels. On the contrary, in a narrow outcrop, local symmetrical tilting around a NW –SE direction can be observed in series overlying the magmatic rocks, indicating prob- ably that the latter form here a thin dyke. Moreover, levels overlying magmatic rocks are baked or affected by hydrothermal phenomenon, showing that the basic rocks were intruded within the sedimentary formations. Anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility measurements (Djellit et al., submitted for publication ) confirmed the intrusive character of these rocks: subhorizontal magnetic foliation obtained in some sites indicates emplacement as sill but subvertical magnetic foliation on the contrary characterizes intrusion as dyke in other sites. Thermal or AF demagnetizations were performed on all samples. Because of the strong mineralogical changes during the heating, AF demag- netization gets better results than the thermal one. During the demagnetization process, the magnetization direction of samples evolves mostly along great circles (remagnetization circles), which shows superimposition of the unblocking temperature (or unblocking fields) spectra for at least two re manent magnetization components ( Fig. 6 ). During thermal demagnetization, the overlapping of unblocking temperature spectra is limited to temperature lower than the Curie temperature of the titanomaghemite. It is therefore due to the presence of both titanomaghemite and magnetite. However, most of the samples do not allow defining a direction after demagnetization of the titanomaghemite because their remanent magnetization carried by magnetite has too weak intensity. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: setting The “Djebel Berga ” area (~ 26° 40'N, 1° 50'E) is located in the “Ahnet” basin, central Sahara ( Fig. 1 ). It corresponds to a structural basin with a NW –SE-trending axis and a ﬂat base ( Fig. 1 ). In its southeastern terminal curvature, the dip is towards the north-west with a low plunge (5° on average), while on its western and eastern narrow ﬂanks, strata dip with a higher angle (20° on average), toward the north-east and the south-west respectively. In the central part of the basin, the beds become horizontal. The northern part of the basin is unconformably overlain by tabular Lower Cretaceous levels called “Continental Intercalaire ” (Kilian, 1922 ). In this basin, two Upper Carboniferous series outcrop: - The lower one (about 350 m thick) is the marine “Djebel Berga ” limestones of late Visean –lower Namurian age—i.e. Serpukhovian, according to Conrad and Legrand Blain (1971) . It includes at the base an alternation of limestones and sandstones, overlain by massive calcareous beds containing brachiopods (Gigantoproduc- tus) and polyparies, interbedded with levels of ﬁne sandstones and claystones (Conrad, 1973; Fabre, 1976). - The upper series is the continental red “Hassi Bachir ” Formation (about 250 m thick) of Upper Namurian –Lower Moscovian age (Conrad, 1973; Con

These studies have demonstrated the importance of widespread secondary magnetizations, mostly remagnetizations of Permian and Cenozoic ages ( Henry et al., 2004a ). Furthermore, the determination of several new paleomagnetic poles has greatly improved the African APWP from the Lower Carboniferous to Dogger times (see Mérabet et al., 2005and references in;Derder et al., 2006and references in). Although these new data are reliable and satisfy modern criteria of paleomagnetic studies, the age of magnetization, in most cases, has not been well constrained by paleomagnetic tests, particularly fold tests (which are actually s.s. tilt tests— see Borradaile, 1997). This underlines the importance of investigations in folded areas over cratonic regions. Another aspect of these earlier studies was that the folding of the Paleozoic sedimentary cover in the Central Sahara platform was considered in general to occur mainly in the Hercynian (e.g. Conrad, 1984; Fabre, 1988; Haddoum et al., 2001 ). Another aspect of these earlier studies was that the folding of the Paleozoic sedimentary cover in the Central Sahara platform was considered in general to occur mainly in the Hercynian (e.g. Conrad, 1984; Fabre, 1988; Haddoum et al., 2001 ). However a recent paleomagnetic study demonstrated the relative importance of the Mesozoic folding phase in the eastern part of the “Reggane” basin (Fig. 1)( Smith et al., 2006 ). In the neighboring “Ahnet” basin ( Fig. 1), Daly and Irving (1983) isolated both a primary magnetization and a Permian remagnetization (i.e. a pre-tilting magnetization and a magnetization acquired between the two folding phases) in the folded Carboniferous “Hassi Bachir ” Formation. This formation provides an excellent opportunity to determine whether the Mesozoic folding was a local event, limited to the “Reggane” basin or whether it affected other Saharan basins as well. The implications of such a result could be of major importance, in particular for petroleum research. For this reason we reinvestigate the “Hassi Bachir” Formation by extending the sampling to include sites covering a larger area and showing various dips in order to allow for a tilt test. We also con- ducted a preliminary paleomagnetic study on the underlying “Djebel Berga” limestone, which is attributed to the Lower Namurian. It corresponds to a structural basin with a NW –SE-trending axis and a ﬂat base ( Fig. 1 ). In its southeastern terminal curvature, the dip is towards the north-west with a low plunge (5° on average), while on its western and eastern narrow ﬂanks, strata dip with a higher angle (20° on average), toward the north-east and the south-west respectively.
